presentingComplaint: Brought by daughter after a brief episode of slurred speech and right-sided facial droop the previous evening, now fully resolved.
history: Frail, independent-with-aids 84-year-old woman living alone. Yesterday around 7pm, while watching television, she abruptly developed slurred speech and drooping of the right side of the mouth with clumsiness of the right hand; she could not name objects for a few minutes. Her neighbour noticed and stayed with her. Symptoms resolved completely within roughly 20-25 minutes and she went to bed, attributing it to tiredness. No headache, no loss of consciousness, no limb jerking, no incontinence, no tongue-biting, no visual aura or scintillations, no chest pain or palpitations at the time. Daughter visited this morning, was told of the event, and brought her in. Background: long-standing hypertension, type 2 diabetes on metformin, a previous minor TIA-like episode 3 years ago (never investigated), and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation documented on a GP ECG last year for which anticoagulation was declined by the patient. Frailty with slow gait and one fall in the past 6 months. Not currently on any antithrombotic. No recent infection, dysuria or fever.
examination: Alert, orientated, comfortable. Neurological examination now entirely normal: cranial nerves intact with symmetrical face, no dysarthria or dysphasia, power 5/5 throughout, normal coordination, gait cautious but no focal deficit. No carotid bruit audible. Pulse irregularly irregular. No signs of infection; chest clear, abdomen soft, no urinary symptoms. Clinically frail (Rockwood ~5).
imaging: CT head (non-contrast): age-related involutional change and small-vessel white-matter hypodensities; no acute infarct or haemorrhage. MRI brain with DWI: no restricted diffusion / no acute infarct; chronic lacunes in left basal ganglia. Carotid Doppler: 30-40% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery, right <30%.
microbiology: Not applicable; no evidence of infection (urinalysis clear, afebrile).
differentialDiagnoses: Transient ischaemic attack (cardioembolic, paroxysmal AF; left hemisphere)
Minor ischaemic stroke with early symptom resolution
Focal seizure with post-ictal (Todd's) speech disturbance
finalDiagnosis: Transient ischaemic attack (high-risk, cardioembolic in the context of untreated paroxysmal atrial fibrillation) - ABCD2 score 6 (age >=60, BP >=140/90, speech disturbance with unilateral weakness, duration 10-59 min, diabetes).
citations: NICE - Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management (NG128) - 2022
AHA/ASA - Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and TIA - 2021
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Ischemic Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective vascular presentation; no antimicrobial therapy indicated.
contraindications: Avoid delaying antithrombotic/anticoagulation assessment; balance high embolic risk against falls and bleeding risk in frailty
Do not give thrombolysis - deficit fully resolved, no acute infarct
Review renal function before dosing DOAC
edgeCases: Complete symptom resolution with normal DWI can still be a TIA; tissue-negative does not exclude the diagnosis
Delayed presentation in a frail elderly patient risks under-triage despite high ABCD2 and untreated AF
Prior undiagnosed AF with declined anticoagulation markedly raises recurrent-stroke risk
Distinguish from focal seizure (no post-ictal drowsiness, no automatisms) and hypoglycaemia (normal glucose)
expectedMaiK: Transient, fully-resolving focal neurological deficit (dysarthria, right facial weakness, transient dysphasia) of sudden onset with negative DWI in an elderly patient with untreated paroxysmal AF - a high-risk cardioembolic TIA requiring urgent secondary prevention.
expectedNextQuestions: Exact time of onset, duration and complete resolution of symptoms?
Any jerking, tongue-biting, incontinence or post-event drowsiness (to exclude seizure)?
Capillary glucose at the time of the episode?
Is she on any anticoagulation/antiplatelet, and why was anticoagulation declined?
Any preceding visual aura, headache or prior similar episodes?
expectedInvestigations: Urgent non-contrast CT head then MRI brain with DWI
12-lead ECG plus prolonged/ambulatory cardiac monitoring for paroxysmal AF
Bloods: capillary and lab glucose, HbA1c, FBC, U&E, lipid profile, coagulation
regressionAssertions: stewardship.tier is null and antibiotics empty
MRI DWI and cardiac monitoring recommended
AF flagged as cardioembolic source warranting anticoagulation assessment
